title: Chapter 45: The Usual Desk, Part 3 of 5: Nothing, Sir
html:
She came out of him slowly, the way you come up out of deep water, and opened her eyes in the white room.
Nothing had changed. The Ash-lamp in its cage on the wall burned white and steady. The jars stood on their shelf by the door with their lids off, waiting. The old man sat folded in the strapped chair with his arms round his knees, and his bare blue feet, and the bruise on his face going black.
Her hand was still on his temple.
She took it away.
And in her hand, in her bare palm, the face lay. She could not see it. Nobody could have seen it. But she could feel it, the way you feel a coin in your fist with your eyes shut. Small and round and warm. Warmer than her hand. Warmer than anything in that white room. A girl's face, in the red light, from under a gray cap, looking at a man as if he mattered.
The jars stood on the shelf by the door.
That was what you did next. That was the second half of the work, and you had to be quick, because a memory out of its owner did not keep. You stood up, and went to the shelf, and held your hand over the mouth of a jar, and opened your fingers, and let it go. And it went down into the glass like a drop of light, and settled, and glowed. And you put the lid on, and wrote the label, and it went to the Inquisitor's desk. And from there to wherever such things went.
If you were not quick, it did not go into the jar. It went into you.
Wren sat in the chair with no straps and held the face in her closed hand, and did not get up.
She counted. One. Two. Three.
At ten, she felt it begin to go. Not out. In. The warmth went out of her palm and up her wrist, slowly, like the warmth of a cup of tea going up your arm on a winter morning. Up the inside of her arm. Into her shoulder. Into her chest.
At twenty, it was in her chest.
At thirty, it was gone from her hand, and her palm was cold again, and empty, and there was a girl's face somewhere inside Wren Halloway, at the back of a small dark cupboard of her own that she had not known she had, in the warmest part of the light. Looking out.
She would have it now. For the rest of her life. A face she had never seen, looking at her as if she mattered.
And the old man would never have it again.
She looked at him.
He had not moved. He sat with his arms round his knees and his eyes on the floor. His finger lifted, on his knee, and fell. Twice. Hold. He did not know that anything had gone. He would never know. There was nobody left in that house to notice that the light under the cupboard door had gone out.
Wren put her glove back on.
She did it very carefully, a finger at a time, smoothing the white kid down over each one, and doing up the small pearl button at the wrist. Then she picked up the tin bowl of cold soup from the floor, and stirred it with the spoon, and broke the skin on it, and held the spoon out.
"Wick," she said. "Eat."
The old man looked at the spoon.
Then, slowly, as if from very far away, his hand came out from round his knees, and took it.
He did not eat. He held it. He looked at it in his hand, the way he had looked at his scraps of paper on the pile.
Wren stood up.
She went to the shelf by the door, and took down one of the glass jars, and put the lid on it, empty, and wrote on the label in her small square upright hand: Wick. Room nine. Wednesday. Nil.
Then she went out, and shut the door behind her, and slid the little wooden shutter across, the way it had been.
The Long Office had not changed either. Forty desks. Twelve windows. The cadets on their bench. Somebody coughing. Pens scratching. The lamps floating on their chains overhead like jellyfish. Nobody looked at her as she walked up between the desks with the empty jar in her gloved hand. Nobody ever did, when an Inquisitor came out of a reading room. It was not polite.
The door at the end was open.
Kross was at his desk, writing. A cup of tea was steaming at his elbow. Another cup stood on the other side of the desk, by the visitors' chair, with a saucer on top of it to keep it warm.
He did not look up when she came in.
"Shut the door, Wren."
She shut it.
"Sit down. Your tea's there."
She sat down in the chair nobody ever sat in. She put the jar on the green leather of the desk, between them. Empty. With its lid on. With its label turned toward him.
Kross went on writing for a while. Then he put down his pen, and took off his spectacles, and folded them, and looked at the jar.
He read the label.
He did not say anything.
He picked the jar up, and turned it round in his long careful fingers, slowly, and held it up to the light from the window, as if there might be something in it after all, something very small that she had missed. There was nothing. The gray river light came through the clear glass and fell on the desk in a little ring.
He put it down.
"Nil," he said.
"Yes, sir."
"Nothing at all?"
"Nothing that could be used, sir." Wren kept her hands folded on her knees. She kept her face where it was. A wall. "He's been emptied to the walls. A long time ago. Years. Every room. There's nothing left in him but one thing, very deep down. A field in the snow. A battle line. From the war, I think. A drum, beating two." She paused. "It's the only thing they left him. I didn't take it. Nobody could use it. It's just—fear. Standing still."
"Hold," said Kross.
Wren did not move.
"Two is hold," said the Inquisitor pleasantly. "In the old drum calls. Did you know? The Commonwealth Foot used them. Before your time. Before mine, nearly." He picked up his tea and drank. "Our friend Sergeant Moll could tell you all about them. Perhaps tomorrow you'll ask him."
"Yes, sir."
"And nothing else? No face? Nothing from this week?" He put the cup down. "Forty people walked past that man every day, Wren. Fed him. Talked over him. Carried a man with a bad leg in and out under his nose. And he kept none of it?"
"There was a little room, sir." She heard her own voice. It was quite steady. It was the voice she used for reports. "Near the front. A cupboard, really. Under the stair. Where the last few days would be, if they were anywhere." She looked at him across the desk. "I opened it. It was dark."
Kross looked at her.
He looked at her for a long time. She did not know how long. She counted, without meaning to, and lost count at nineteen, and did not start again. The fire ticked in the grate. Outside the tall window, far down, a barge horn sounded on the river, long and low, and stopped.
She did not look away.
She thought of the old Inquisitor with no eyebrows, at the Academy, who had taught her that a still face was not enough. They'll look at your eyes, girl. The good ones always do. A wall's no use if there's a window in it. And she thought of the girl's face, at the back of her own small dark cupboard. Looking out. And she made her eyes look out of her own face the way that girl's eyes had looked out of hers. Straight. Dark. Steady. As if the person across the desk was only a person.
Kross smiled.
"Well," he said. "Then he's no use to us."
He picked up his pen again.
"Send him down to the Health," he said, writing. "The Office of Public Health keeps a house for the simple ones. Out past the tanneries. Under-Secretary Pallister's people will fetch him this afternoon, if you send a boy with a note. They're very good with old men like that. Very kind. They give them sweets."
Wren sat in the chair.
She thought of a crypt she had never seen, under a church on a hill, that she had read about in one of Watcher Fisk's reports. Parish of St Bride's. The doctor Silas keeps the drained children of the parish in the crypt. Fifty-odd. Sweet breath. The Health has the matter under review.
She thought of the old man in room nine, holding his spoon.
"Sir," she said.
Kross went on writing.
"Yes, Wren?"
She opened her mouth.
And she understood, sitting there in the chair that nobody ever sat in, with her tea going cold under its saucer, that this was the test. Not the face. Not the jar. This. Whether she would say Sir, don't send him to the Health. Whether she would say Sir, I've read the reports about the sweets. Whether she would say anything at all about an old man who could not be used, to a man who had written in a file, in a small neat hand, A pity. He was proud.
If she said it, he would know.
If she did not say it, Wick would go to the Health.
She closed her mouth.
"Nothing, sir," she said. "I'll send a boy."
"Thank you, Wren."
He did not look up.
She stood, and picked up her cup of tea, and took the saucer off it, and drank it. All of it. It was hot and strong and very sweet, the way he liked it, the way he always made it for her, and it burned her mouth, and she drank it anyway, standing by his desk, because if she put it down she was afraid he would see her hand.
Then she put the cup down on its saucer, very quietly, and went out, and shut the door.
She wrote the note for the Health at her desk. Four lines. To the Office of Public Health, Under-Secretary Pallister's department, with the Inquisitor's compliments. One old man, simple, known as Wick. No family. No use. To be collected from the Office, room nine, at their convenience.
She sealed it. She gave it to the messenger boy at the door, a child of eleven with a runny nose, and a copper for himself.
And then she sat down at her usual desk, and opened a folder, and laid it flat in front of her. And under the edge of the folder, in her lap, where nobody walking down the Long Office could see, she took the gray book out of her pocket and opened it at the back. She could not wait for tonight. It would fade by tonight. They always faded, a little, by night. She would copy it out later, by candlelight, into a new black book, and paste a label on its spine. 482.
She wrote, small, quickly, the way she always did:
Wick. Rag-and-bone man. Room nine.
Left him: a field in the snow. A line of men. A drum beating two. He holds.
Took: a girl's face. Short dark hair, cut with a knife. Gray cap too big. Red light. Looking at him as if he were a man. He kept it at the back, where it was warm.
She stopped. She looked at the last line for a long time.
Then she wrote, under it, in the same hand:
Not in a jar. In me. I'll keep it for him.
And closed the book, and put it back in her pocket, and turned the page of the folder on her desk, and read it, and did not see a word.
Rowan at Noon
At noon the Long Office ate.
Not at the desks. Mr. Abernethy did not allow food at the desks. Crumbs got into the files, he said, and grease got onto the paper, and once, forty years ago, a clerk called Pocket had dropped a pickled onion into a report on the Archon's cousin, and the report had smelled of vinegar for the rest of its life. So at the noon bell the clerks and the watchers and the cadets got up from their desks and their bench and went out through a narrow door at the back of the Long Office, into a room that everybody called the Pantry, though there had never been any food kept in it.
It was a long bare room with a stone floor and one window, high up, too high to see out of. There was a long table down the middle with benches on either side, and a stove at one end with a big black kettle on it that was always just coming to the boil and never quite getting there. You brought your own food. Bread and cheese, mostly. Cold sausage. An apple, if you were rich. The watchers ate standing up, by the stove, talking in low voices about the night. The clerks ate sitting down, in silence, with their books open beside their plates. The Inquisitors did not come into the Pantry at all. They ate in their own rooms, or went out to the chophouse on Chancery Lane, or did not eat.
Wren came into the Pantry.
She had never done it before. Not once in two years and five months. She did not know why she did it today. She only knew that she could not sit at her usual desk any longer, with the folders, and the reading-room doors along the wall, and the fifth one from the end with its little shutter slid across. And she could not go into the Inquisitor's room. And she could not go out, into the snow, because then someone would write down that she had gone out.
So she came into the Pantry.
The room went quiet.
Not all at once. The way the Long Office had gone quiet for Kross that morning. From the door inward. The watchers by the stove stopped talking. The clerks at the long table looked up from their books, and then down again, quickly. Somebody put down a cup.
Wren did not look at any of them. She went to the end of the long table, the far end, where it was nearest the window and coldest and nobody ever sat, and sat down on the bench, and took her bread and cheese out of her pocket, wrapped in a piece of brown paper, and unwrapped it, and looked at it.
After a moment the room began to talk again. Lower than before.
Somebody sat down on the bench across from her.
She looked up.
It was Rowan Thorne.
He sat very straight, the way the cadets were taught to sit, with his back like a ramrod and his hands flat on the table on either side of his plate. He had a plate. That was the first thing she noticed. A real plate, white china, with a blue line round the rim, and on it a slice of pie. Pork pie, with a thick gold crust, and the jelly shining at the edges. Nobody else in the Pantry had a plate.
He saw her looking at it.
"The Inquisitor sends it," he said. "Every day. From the chophouse." His face was stiff. "He says a boy who's growing needs his dinner."
Wren did not say anything.
Rowan looked at the pie. He did not eat it. He had a barley sugar in his cheek still, she could see the bump of it, and his hands on the table on either side of the plate were very still. Long hands. Thin. Too old for the rest of him. The knuckles were scraped.
"You were in room nine," he said.
"Yes."
"With the old man. The one they brought in a cart." He looked at the pie. "I saw them carry him up the stair. He was making a noise."
"Yes."
"Was there anything? In him?"
Wren looked at him across the table. At the pale stiff face that was trying so hard. At the eyes.
She had them now. Those eyes. At the back of her own small cupboard, in the warm light. She could feel them there, looking out. And here was the same pair, across a table in the Pantry, in a different face. Younger. Angrier. More afraid.
"No," she said. "Nothing."
Rowan nodded slowly. As if that was what he had expected. As if that was what he had hoped.
Then he put his hand into the pocket of his gray cadet's coat and took something out and put it on the table between them. Next to his plate. Small. White. Hard.
A folded wrapper. The size of a fingernail. So tight and so neat and so sharp at every corner that it might have been carved out of ivory.
"Look," he said. "I can do it now. All the way. Eleven."
Wren looked at it.
"He showed me," said Rowan. "The first day. Two years ago. When I came up the stair for the first time and didn't know where to sit, and everybody was looking at me, because of the name." His voice was very flat. "He came out of his room and gave me a barley sugar and showed me how to fold the wrapper. Small. He said, When you don't know what to do with your hands, Cadet, fold something. It keeps the face still." Rowan looked at the little white square. "I could only do seven. For a year. Then nine. Then ten." He paused. "I did eleven last night. For the first time. In my room. At the Academy. With the lamp out."
"That's very good," said Wren.
"It's not good. It's folding paper." Rowan's mouth went thin. "But I wanted somebody to see it." He did not look at her. "I wanted to show him, this morning. And then I didn't. I don't know why. He'd have been pleased."
Wren looked at the wrapper on the table, and then at the boy.
"Why me?" she said.
Rowan was quiet for a moment.
"Because you were there," he said. "At the grating. A week ago. On Wednesday." He kept his eyes on the wrapper. "You said right. And he went left. And I heard the word. The one in the dark. The one that went through everybody like a bell. And then the Inquisitor asked me if I'd heard which way it came from, and I said—" He stopped.
"You said your ears were still ringing," said Wren.
"Yes."
"Why?"
Rowan looked up.
And for one moment, across the long table in the Pantry, with the kettle failing to boil on the stove behind them and the clerks eating in silence with their books open and the window too high to see out of, the stiff pale face stopped trying. It went still. Not the way hers went still, not a wall. The other way. The way a pond goes still when the wind drops, so that you can see right down to the bottom.
"Because he's with her," he said. "Isn't he. Corin Vane. He's with my sister."
Wren did not answer.
"Everybody in the Office knows it," said Rowan. "Nobody says it to me. They stop talking when I come in." His long scraped hands pressed flat on the table. "And I thought, at the grating, if I say left, they'll catch him. In a sewer. Today. And wherever he was going, they'll find that too. And she'll be there." He stopped. "And I didn't know yet if I wanted her found. I still don't know. So I said my ears were ringing. So that I'd have longer to decide."
His right hand came up off the table, without his seeming to notice, and lay flat against the front of his gray coat. On his chest. Over the place where, under the coat, under the tunic, against his skin, a letter had lain for a year. Cream paper, cheap. Crumpled. With another boy's blood on it.
Wren looked at the hand, and did not say that she knew what was under it.
"That's not a reason anybody would put in a report," she said at last.
"No." Rowan took his hand away from his chest, and picked up the folded wrapper, and put it back in his pocket. "That's why I'm telling you, and not him."
He picked up his fork and began, at last, to eat his pie.
Wren ate her bread and cheese.
After a while, without looking up from his plate, Rowan said, "I'm to stand at the door tomorrow. When the sergeant comes. Moll. The Inquisitor says it will be good for me to watch." He cut a piece of pie. "Watch what, I asked him. He said, How an honest man lies, Cadet. There is no better lesson in the world."
Wren went on eating.
"Is the sergeant an honest man?" said Rowan.
"I don't know," said Wren. "I've never met him."
Rowan nodded. As if that, too, was what he had expected.
He finished his pie. He wiped his mouth with his handkerchief, and folded the handkerchief, very neatly, and put it away. Then he stood up from the bench, with his back like a ramrod, and picked up the white plate with the blue line round it, to take it back to the chophouse boy at the door.
"Halloway," he said.
"Yes?"
"You hum." He looked down at her. "When you're copying. At your desk. I've heard you, from the bench. Three notes. Over and over." He frowned a little. "Did you know?"
Wren looked up at him.
"No," she said. "I don't hum."
Rowan looked at her for a moment longer. Then he nodded, as if she had told him something, and went away down the Pantry with his plate, past the watchers by the stove, and out.
